content.title: Response to rebuttal
content.comment:
Thank you to the authors for the response to my review.

Thank you for the clarification four EditTTS and adding comparisons to EditSpeech. 

>  On the other hand, our work proposed a VAE-based method to edit speech based on context information, which may be useful for other AI applications like image editing, video editing, and even RL for decision-making, as these fields require efficient context information usage. Therefore, we submitted this paper to the corresponding topic (Applications (eg, speech processing, computer vision, NLP)).

A typical ICLR paper that offers a general purpose algorithm will present results across multiple tasks.

The claim that this has broad applicability would be stronger if you presented results on some of these tasks.

> We apologize for the delayed update and the inconvenience it has caused. The audio samples, which include partial inference vs. Entire inference with different editing systems and ablation studies, are now available at http://bitly.ws/uMFd.

Thank you. The entire inference samples are obviously better than partial inference, and EditSpeech seems to perform the task poorly.

However, I'm surprised that no cross-utterance examples were demonstrated -- showing that the CU context was resolving some ambiguity over prosody of the infilling. Why are these not provided, or if the examples have CU context, why is the CU context not listed?

> In addition, we lack sufficient time to reproduce CampNet, which has no public code. To our knowledge, CampNet also employs partial inference with an encoder-decoder based on multi-head attention. However, our method adds context information, a conditional VAE module, a duration predictor and adjustor, etc., so we believe it has the potential to perform better in naturalness and prosody expressiveness.

It is unfortunate there is not an open implementation of CampNet and that you do not have time to reproduce it. I believe [the demos of partial inference from CampNet are pretty good](https://hairuo55.github.io/CampNet/) despite teh fact that they do not do full resynthesis of the utterance. Without a comparison, I don't believe we can say this work pushes SOTA on this somewhat specific task. (Which would boost its relevance to ICLR)

> Technical and Empirical Novelty And Significance

I still feel that, as an applications paper, this could use stronger baseline to compare against and that it is not of broad interest to the ICLR community as it is speech centric. Therefore I still stand by my initial scores.

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
Thanks for the review and for noting that "The paper targets an open problem that is usually ignored in earlier papers". The reviewer’s main concern is that

> In Table 1, similarity scores are lower in the proposed system, subjective scores might be suggesting that the reconstruction of the unmasked regions is not perfect as compared to copying them. Table 4 suggests that not including that loss deteriorates the objective scores (1:1 vs 0:1). It might have been better if there were some discussion on this.

Thanks for pointing out the seemingly contradictory subjective and objective results. We apologize for the misunderstanding caused by the stacking of metrics in the original Table, which has been divided into Tables 1 and 3 for better illustration. 

Note that it is because ground truth audios do not contain the edited audio, we manually spliced the audio waveform for the editing operations, and the MOS similarity score of Wave_cut serves as an upper bound indicator. Wave_cut is not an effective editing method, as it is time-consuming and labor-intensive for audio workers and has the lowest score in terms of consistency.

Meanwhile, Tables 1 and 3 indicate that our proposed method achieved comparable performance on subjective MOS similarity scores and objective reconstruction scores, compared to Mel_cut (which directly copies the mel-spectrogram in the unmasked regions), demonstrating our model's ability to restore the mel-spectrogram.

Additionally,  the entire inference was utilized in ablation experiments with varying loss ratios. Since the input mel-spectrogram of speech editing models is discontinuous, only the unmasked region is included; therefore, when the loss ratio is 1:1, the reconstruction results of masked regions contain more noise than those of unmasked regions. At the same time, we set a high mask proportion (50%), so this could also result in loss ratio(1:1) having a poorer reconstruction performance than loss ratio(1:1.5) throughout the entire inference. On the other hand, loss ratio of 0:1 indicates that the loss of unmasked regions was not calculated during training, but that the unmasked area was generated by the editing system during entire inference, resulting in the worst reconstruction performance for loss ratio 0:1.

> Details of the some experimental models might be missing. For example, it has not been mentioned how the speaker embeddings are obtained. How did the setting quantize the estimated duration? Is it based on rounding?

Thanks for the advice and we have added additional configuration details. In Section 4.2, we added that the speaker embedding is a lookup table mapping each speaker id to a specific 256-dim vector; the duration predictor consists of two 1D convolutional blocks with ReLU activation, followed by layer normalization with a 0.1 dropout rate, and an extra linear layer to predict the duration of each phoneme; also in Section 3.1, the estimated duration is rounded after the duration predictor and the adjustor. Besides, we will release our code if the paper is accepted. 

> Is the context size important for the success? Would having only 1-2 utterances suffice?

We followed the setting of [Li et al. (2022)](https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.30/), which suggests that TTS system with 5 utterances achieve higher MOS scores than systems with 1 or 3 utterances, and only marginal MOS improvements were obtained using more than 5 neighbouring utterances.

In the revised paper, experiments on $L=2$ were added. The reconstruction metrics suggest that  $L=5$ can enhance the capability of reconstruction.

| System | FFE       | MCD       | WER       |
| ------ | --------- | --------- | --------- |
| L = 0  | 0.333     | 6.750     | 5.503     |
| L = 2  | 0.332     | 6.697     | 5.392     |
| L = 5  | **0.327** | **6.657** | **5.377** |

We apologize for not having enough time to find enough volunteers to score subjectively, but the audio examples are available (http://bitly.ws/uMFd), $L=5$ has better naturalness and expressiveness, consistent with the objective results.

>It might be better to make it clear that the paper is doing text based speech editing.

Thanks for the advice. We restated the introduction, method description, and conclusion.

>Technical and Empirical Novelty And Significance

We apologize for making an unclear claim about our novelties and contributions.  In this paper, we proposed a VAE-based method to extract information from the cross-utterances, which could better reconstruct speech for editing and thoroughly avoid the problem of non-smooth boundaries. This is different from the research that has been done in the past on how to smooth the prosody of boundaries. In addition, unlike the mask training loss function utilized in speech, images, and text, which only focus on the mask portion, we propose a biased loss function, and the effect is well verified on a challenging dataset.

Many thanks for pointing out the typos, we fixed them.

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
Thanks for the review and for noting that this paper is a ''clearly written contribution to an existing problem and is technically sound, including good analysis and ablations''. Regarding the question:

>It's not clear how MOS similarity is calculated. There do not appear to be reference utterances. Is this similarity to a reference utterance to the target speaker?

For the experiments involving the editing scenarios (deletion, insertion, and replacement), the volunteers were instructed to evaluate the MOS similarity by comparing the **unedited** portion of the synthesized speech to the reference audio. For example, volunteers rated the MOS similarity of the part "go down" when the original utterance of the ground truth was "Can't you go down?" and the edited utterance of synthesized speech was "Please go down." These experiments were designed to demonstrate that when semantic information changes, it may not be prudent to blindly pursue audio similarity. 

For the experiments in the reconstruction scenario, the volunteers were instructed to compare the whole-speech similarity (both the **edited and unedited** parts). The purpose of these tests was to confirm that our proposed method can also reconstruct audio by restoring the prosody and rhythmic characteristics of the target speaker.

>  The paper could be improved by a comparison to more competitive contrasting systems, e.g. VoCo. Also a more thorough discussion of the impact of the reduced similarity scores (in addition to a more detailed discussion of the performance here).

In the revised version of our paper, we included a comparison to [EditSpeech](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9688051/), which was published after VoCo and improved the prosody near the boundary by bidirectional fusion. Table1's subjective MOS score for speech editing and Table3's reconstruction metrics demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baseline in terms of both naturalness and reconstruction performance.

>Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

We corrected some typos, added additional configuration details, and performed a more detailed analysis of the experimental results. For instance, we added the details of the duration predictor, split Table 1 in the original version into Tables 1 and 3 for better interpretation, and conducted additional ablation studies on the impact of fewer context details.

>Ethics Concerns: Since speech editing can be used for deep fake generation, I would expect this paper to include an ethics statement. However, it does not include one.

We have included a discussion of the broader effect of speech editing at the conclusion of our revised paper, and we apologize for not including an ethics statement in a timely manner. 

Text-based speech editing can reduce the workload of voice editors and content creators, among other societal benefits, as discussed in the paper. Our speech editing and reconstruction experiments were conducted under the assumption that the model user is the intended speaker and has been approved by the speaker. 

However, when the model is generalized to unseen speakers, it increases the risk of unauthorized audio modification and can subsequently be used to disseminate false information. Consequently, the relevant key components should be accompanied by the model of speech editing, including the protocol to ensure that the speaker agrees to execute the modification and the system to detect the edited speech.

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
Many thanks for the reviewers' valuable suggestions to our paper. We kindly write this comment to address the concerns.

>The experimental results are difficult to interpret as the task of speech editing is nascent and does not have strong baselines yet.  Experiments do not compare to other published work on this task (CampNet, EditSpeech, EdiTTS).

It is true that speech editing is still in its infancy and lacks solid benchmarks.

During our research, we have noticed [EdiTTS](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.02584v3.pdf), but the content replacement task studied in this paper is distinct from general text-based speech editing tasks, which aim to combine multiple TTS-generated audios. Its [input](https://github.com/neosapience/editts/blob/e612807e84c71cd30a09cf880b83c6b5e5a47b88/resources/filelists/edit_content_example.txt) consists of two sentences of text without taking into account a real-world audio sample. As revealed in the  [code](https://github.com/neosapience/editts/blob/e612807e84c71cd30a09cf880b83c6b5e5a47b88/model/tts.py#L285), EdiTTS generates coherent audio by fusing hidden variables $\mu$ derived from the phonomes of the two sentences. Consequently, we cannot directly replace one of the audios synthesized by TTS with real-world audio, nor can we deduce corresponding hidden variable $\mu$ from the real audio.

We now add a comparison of our system to [EditSpeech](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9688051/). This baseline utilized partial inference and bidirectional fusion. Its VCTK-trained audio samples (44 hours of audio from 109 speakers) can be found at <https://daxintan-cuhk.github.io/EditSpeech/.> We conducted the comparison under similar circumstances, including the structure details of the text encoder, speaker encoder, length regulator, duration predictor, and vocoder.

In our revised paper, Table1 and Table3 compare the objective reconstruction performance and subjective results of naturalness and similarity. The results demonstrate that our proposed system using either partial or complete inference is more natural than EditSpeech. Meanwhile, since partial inference directly copies the actual mel-spectrogram of the unedited region, it is reasonable that partial inference had superior reconstruction performance with regard to similarity and mel-cepstral distortion (MCD). Nevertheless, our system still outperforms EditSpeech in terms of F0 frame error (FFE) and word error rates (WER).

In addition, we lack sufficient time to reproduce [CampNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09950), which has no public code. To our knowledge,  CampNet also employs partial inference with an encoder-decoder based on multi-head attention. However, our method adds context information, a conditional VAE module, a duration predictor and adjustor, etc., so we believe it has the potential to perform better in naturalness and prosody expressiveness.

>Without audio samples, I cannot get a sense for how well this method works in practice.

We apologize for the delayed update and the inconvenience it has caused.  The audio samples, which include partial inference vs. Entire inference with different editing systems and ablation studies, are now available at <http://bitly.ws/uMFd>.

>The overall relevance of this method is limited to the narrow application area of speech editing, and it feels like this work is more appropriate for a speech conference.

Our work focuses on speech processing, which is likely to obtain more impact at a speech conference. But we missed this year's top speech conference submission deadline (e.g., InterSpeech, ICASSP). On the other hand, our work proposed a VAE-based method to edit speech based on context information, which may be useful for other AI applications like image editing, video editing, and even RL for decision-making, as these fields require efficient context information usage. Therefore, we submitted this paper to the corresponding topic  (Applications (eg, speech processing, computer vision, NLP)).

>Technical and Empirical Novelty And Significance

We apologize that our claim of novelty and significance was not clear. In order to better reconstruct speech for editing and completely avoid the problem of non-smooth boundaries, we propose a VAE-based method to extract information from the cross-utterances. This is distinct from previous studies that have investigated boundary smoothing techniques. We also propose a biased loss function, and the effect is well verified on a large multi-speaker dataset, in contrast to the mask training loss function used in speech, images, and text, which only focuses on the mask portion.

Many thanks for pointing out the typos and inaccuracies; we have corrected them.

content.title: Authors response
content.comment:
We are appreciative of the reviewer's useful comments, which have helped us to improve our paper effectively.  The reviewer has the following concerns:

> Some more ablation consideration, limitation discussion, and quantitative result interpretation would make the paper even stronger.

We have added a series of additional experiments and interpretations. First, we add a baseline [EditSpeech](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9688051/) system to compare subjective and objective metrics, which utilized partial inference and bidirectional fusion. Table1 gives a subjective MOS score for speech editing and Table3 gives reconstruction metrics to demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms the baseline in terms of both naturalness and reconstruction performance. In addition, we conducted an additional ablation study on our system with only 2 utterances, and the results are shown in Table4. The objective results indicate that using fewer utterances can hinder the capability of reconstruction. The audio examples are available on the website (http://bitly.ws/uMFd). In a few of the examples, we believe that $L=5$ is more natural and expressive than $L=2$, which is consistent with the objective results.

> Reproducibility is not clear down to the last details.

In the revised paper, additional details were provided. For example, we added in the Section 4.2 that the speaker embedding is learned from a 256-dim embedding layer and added to the Transformer output; the duration predictor is made up of two 1D convolutional blocks with ReLU activation, layer normalization with a dropout rate of 0.1, and an additional linear layer to predict the duration of each phoneme. In Section 3.1, following the duration predictor and the adjustor, the estimated duration is rounded.  Besides, we will release our source code if the paper is accepted. 

> Technical Novelty And Significance

We apologize for the unclear claim for our novelty and contributions. Different from the existing research on how to smooth the prosody of boundaries, in this paper, we proposed a VAE-based method to extract information from the context (cross-utterance), which could better reconstruct speech for editing and thoroughly avoid the problem of non-smooth boundaries. Besides,  in contrast to the mask training loss function used in speech, images, and text, which focuses solely on the mask portion, we propose a biased loss function, and the effect is validated on a  dataset.

>Ethics Concerns: Editing of human speech bears major societal and legal implications and contributed potentially to public's "fear of AI"

We have added a discussion of the broader effects of speech editing to the ending of our revised paper and apologize for not including an ethics statement in time. 

In the introduction, we discussed the applications of text-based speech editing that can benefit society, such as video production on social media and game and film dubbing, which require personalized voice requirements and high requirements for voice naturalness. On the other hand, relevant key components should accompany speech editing models, such as the protocol to ensure that the speaker agrees to execute the modification and the system to detect the edited speech.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
A system for speech editing that:
* Attempts to produce consistent in-filling of speech with speaker, context and acoustic features.
* Cross-utterance context is used to improve the editing quality.

Weaknesses

content.summary_of_the_review:
The overall relevance of this method is limited to the narrow application area of speech editing, and it feels like this work is more appropriate for a speech conference.

The experimental results are difficult to interpret as the task of speech editing is nascent and does not have strong baselines yet. The experiments do not seem to compare to other published work on this task.

Without audio samples (as of the review deadline, the demo page said “to be updated”), I cannot get a sense for how well this method works in practice. What I would like to hear are some examples of how previous systems do not correctly change the prosody of the utterance when edited due to only doing partial inference, and how this method fixes those by performing a full resynthesis.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes the use of context from neighboring utterances of the same speaker to better learn the masked parts of the spectrogram for speech editing. The paper also argues that it is also important to estimate the unmasked speech regions and uses a loss function that also tries to minimize the error on the unmasked region with a smaller weight than the masked part. The VAE used in as the editor of the spectrogram is conditioned on the context information and phonetic information. Once the spectrogram is edited, it is converted to audio by a pertained HiFiGAN. Subjective MOS tests show that in terms of naturalness, the proposed approach is better than a manually edited wav version while it is slightly worse in terms of similarity to the original waveform. Objective WER, F0 frame error and mel-cepstral distortion evaluations show that the cross-utterance context and using the additional loss from unmasked loss are important for the model to be successful.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- A significance analysis is provided for the MOS experiments. 
- An ablation study shows the effect of the proposed cross-utterance context and the modified loss function which supports the claims in the introduction.   
- The paper targets an open problem (not simply copy pasting the unmasked regions of audio) that is usually ignored in earlier papers. 

Weaknesses: 
- Details of the some experimental models might be missing. For example, it has not been mentioned how the speaker embeddings are obtained. How did the setting quantize the estimated duration? Is it based on rounding?
- Some experimental results are not well argued. For example, in Table 1, similarity scores are lower in the proposed system. Does this mean that reconstruction of the unmasked regions are not near perfect? This can also be argued based on the fact that wave-cut has better similarity scores.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty: The main novelty is the use of cross-utterance context for the speech editing task. There is also an emphasize on the importance of including the loss due to the unmasked regions but subjective vs. objective scores might be conflicting.  

Quality: Experiments are limited but sufficient. One concern to me is that subjective scores might be suggesting that the reconstruction of the unmasked regions is not perfect as compared to copying them; however, Table 4 suggests that not including that loss deteriorates the objective scores (1:1 vs 0:1). It might have been better if there were some discussion on this. 

Clarity: Mostly clearly written except some typos. Some minor typos or inconsistent notation: Bert should be BERT. CU-CVAE should be used everywhere: some paragraphs have CUC-VAE.

Reproducibility: It uses open datasets, most of the work should be reproducible if a few more details are added such as the speaker embedding model, a better description of the duration model, etc.

Other comments:
- Is the context size important for the success? Would having only 1-2 utterances suffice? 
- SpeechPainter (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.07273.pdf) can be another relevant paper that deals with a similar problem so it might be helpful to check that study.
- It might be better to make it clear that the paper is doing text based speech editing.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper addresses the problem of discontinuity at the boundary between the unedited an edited part of an audio. The VAE based model performs spectrogram editing by using some context from the neighboring utterances as well as a multitask loss that includes the reconstruction of the unmasked region. MOS tests and objective evaluations show improvements but some results may need further discussion. Even though it is well-put together, the paper may benefit from a revision especially with a deeper analysis of the results.

content.title: Cross-utterance Conditioned Coherent Speech Editing via Biased Training and Entire Inference
content.abstract: Text-based speech editing systems are developed to enable users to select, cut, copy and paste speech based on the transcript. Existing state-of-art editing systems based on neural networks do partial inferences with no exception, that is, only generate new words that need to be replaced or inserted. This manner usually leads to the prosody of the edited part being inconsistent with the previous and subsequent speech and the failure to handle the alteration of intonation. To address these problems, we propose a cross-utterance conditioned coherent speech editing system, which first does the entire reasoning at inference time. Benefiting from a cross-utterance conditioned variational autoencoder, our proposed system can forge speech by utilizing speaker information, context and acoustic features, and the mel-spectrogram of unedited fragments from the original audio. Also, we apply biased training to concentrate more attention on the part that needs to be reconstructed throughout training. Experiments conducted on subjective and objective metrics demonstrate that our approach outperforms the partial inference method on various editing operations regarding naturalness and prosody consistency.
